classification.difficultyReason: Choose a general cutting line and connect diagonal bisection with triangle congruence to establish equal side portions, then compare the resulting areas and cover the diagonal case; the prompt supplies no construction or intermediate steps.

content.prompt: Prove that: Any line through the intersection of the diagonals of a parallelogram dissects the parallelogram into two figures of equal area.

answer.short:
The two figures have equal area.

Diagonal bisection and congruent triangles show that the two resulting trapezia have equal parallel sides and the same height.
answer.worked:
Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram whose diagonals intersect at $O$. First suppose the line meets opposite sides $AB$ and $CD$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively, away from the vertices.

The diagonals bisect each other, so $AO=CO$. Also, $\angle AOE=\angle COF$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle OAE=\angle OCF$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel CD$). Therefore $\triangle AOE\equiv\triangle COF$ (AAS), giving $AE=CF$.

Opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal, so $AB=CD$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}EB&=AB-AE\\EB&=CD-CF\\EB&=FD.\end{align*}$$
Let $h$ be the perpendicular distance between $AB$ and $CD$. The two trapezia have areas
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{area}(AEFD)&=\frac12(AE+FD)h,\\\operatorname{area}(EBCF)&=\frac12(EB+CF)h.
\end{align*}$$
Since $AE=CF$ and $FD=EB$, these areas are equal. The same argument applies if the line meets $AD$ and $BC$, after relabelling the vertices.

If the line passes through a vertex, it is a diagonal. Each diagonal divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles (SSS, using equal opposite sides and the common diagonal), so their areas are equal. Thus every line through $O$ gives two figures of equal area.
